reference.source: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice / GeneReviews
clinicalPearls: An autosomal recessive myopathy caused by variants in TRIM32, allelic with limb-girdle muscular dystrophy R8 (formerly LGMD2H), first described in the Hutterite population
Presents with slowly progressive proximal limb-girdle weakness, and mild facial or neck weakness may occur
Onset is usually in early to mid-adulthood, though it can be earlier, and progression is generally slow with prolonged preservation of ambulation
Creatine kinase is often moderately elevated and electromyography shows a myopathic pattern
The muscle biopsy hallmark is dilatation and vacuolation of the sarcotubular system, particularly of type 2 fibres, giving the disease its name
TRIM32 encodes an E3 ubiquitin ligase, and its dysfunction impairs protein turnover in muscle
The phenotype overlaps with other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies, so a broad genetic panel is often required
Diagnosis combines the limb-girdle weakness pattern, the sarcotubular vacuolar biopsy changes, and TRIM32 genetic testing
reference.pathophysiology: Sarcotubular myopathy is caused by recessive variants in TRIM32, which encodes a tripartite-motif E3 ubiquitin ligase that targets specific muscle proteins for degradation through the ubiquitin-proteasome system. Loss of normal TRIM32 function disrupts protein quality control and turnover in skeletal muscle, leading to abnormal accumulation and to dilatation and vacuolation of the sarcotubular (sarcoplasmic reticulum and T-tubule) membranes seen histologically. This membranous disorganisation, preferentially affecting type 2 fibres, produces progressive proximal muscle weakness.
additionalDifferentials: Other limb-girdle muscular dystrophies (calpainopathy, dysferlinopathy, sarcoglycanopathies)
additionalInvestigations: Muscle biopsy with histochemistry and electron microscopy to demonstrate sarcotubular vacuolation
Muscle MRI to characterise the pattern of involvement
Genetic testing with a TRIM32-inclusive limb-girdle muscular dystrophy panel
Cardiac and respiratory assessment as part of neuromuscular evaluation
redFlags: Rapidly progressive or asymmetric weakness suggesting an alternative or inflammatory cause
Respiratory muscle weakness with declining vital capacity
Significant cardiac symptoms prompting cardiac evaluation
Marked dysphagia atypical for the usual phenotype
reference.prognosis: The disorder generally follows a slowly progressive course with proximal weakness, and many patients retain independent walking for many years; life expectancy is usually normal, though monitoring for respiratory involvement is appropriate in advanced disease.
pitfalls: Attributing the presentation to a more common limb-girdle dystrophy without genetic confirmation
Missing the characteristic sarcotubular vacuolation if electron microscopy is not performed
Assuming a dominant inheritance pattern in what is a recessive disorder when counselling families
Overlooking milder facial or neck involvement that can aid recognition
references: Bradley and Daroff Neurology in Clinical Practice
GeneReviews: TRIM32-related limb-girdle muscular dystrophy / sarcotubular myopathy
management: No disease-specific or curative therapy exists, so centre care on maintaining function with individualised physiotherapy to preserve strength and prevent contractures
Provide occupational therapy, orthoses, and mobility aids to sustain independence as proximal weakness progresses
Monitor respiratory function periodically and introduce non-invasive ventilation if nocturnal hypoventilation develops
Undertake cardiac assessment as part of routine neuromuscular surveillance
Coordinate care through a multidisciplinary neuromuscular service
Offer genetic counselling for the autosomal recessive inheritance and arrange testing of at-risk relatives
